findings.title: Reschedule cleanup is not awaited after getCalendar became async
findings.body: After the booking is already updated to CANCELLED, calendar and video cleanup runs in bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...). forEach discards the promise returned by an async callback, so the await getCalendar and the subsequent calendar.deleteEvent / deleteMeeting are not part of Reschedule's completion. The try/catch around the forEach only catches synchronous throws, not rejections from those awaits, which become unhandled rejections. The function then sends the reschedule email and returns true. On a serverless runtime the invocation can finish or freeze before the external calls finish, and because the row is already cancelled this path will not retry. The original calendar event and video meeting can remain, so the slot stays busy and a live meeting is left for a cancelled booking. Await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) or use a for...of loop so both deletes are joined to the handler and failures are caught.

findings.title: WipeMyCal reschedule uses forEach(async) and drops cleanup
findings.body: WipeMyCal reschedule marks the booking CANCELLED, then starts cleanup with bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...) / deleteMeeting(...) }). Array.forEach does not await async callbacks, and the surrounding try/catch cannot see their rejections. The handler continues to sendRequestRescheduleEmail and returns true while Google/Outlook deletion and video deletion are still in flight (or not started, if the runtime suspends first). Failures are unhandled rejections rather than logged errors. A cancelled booking can leave the external event and meeting in place, blocking the time slot. Replace forEach with an awaited Promise.all(map(async ...)) or a for...of loop.

findings.title: requestReschedule does not wait for calendar or video deletion
findings.body: requestReschedule sets the booking to CANCELLED, then calls bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) to await getCalendar and deleteEvent, or to call the now-async deleteMeeting. forEach ignores the callback promise, and nothing after the loop awaits those operations before sendRequestRescheduleEmail and the BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks. There is no try/catch on this loop, so a rejected dynamic import or a failed deleteEvent/deleteMeeting is an unhandled rejection. The mutation still completes successfully. Because the booking is already CANCELLED, the UI will not offer this cancel/reschedule again, and the external calendar event or video meeting can be left behind (double-booking the slot, live meeting for a cancelled booking). Collect the promises with map and await Promise.all before sending email and webhooks.

findings.title: Recurring cancel never joins per-calendar deletes to apiDeletes
findings.body: When cancelling all remaining occurrences, calendar deletion is bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... const deletedEvent = await calendar?.deleteEvent(...); apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); }). forEach does not return those promises. The push happens only after deleteEvent has already settled, and it pushes the resolved value rather than the in-flight promise. The later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) therefore does not wait for this work and cannot observe its failures. The handler still returns "Booking successfully cancelled." The non-recurring branch in the same function was converted to a for...of that pushes calendar.deleteEvent's promise before awaiting; this recurring branch was only given an inner await and still races the request lifetime. Recurring events can remain on connected calendars. Build an array of delete promises (per credential and per updated booking) and await them with the rest of apiDeletes.

findings.title: Eager import() promises load every app and can reject unhandled
findings.body: appStore calls import() for every integration while the module is evaluating, instead of exposing lazy thunks such as () => import("./applecalendar"). The first import of @calcom/app-store therefore starts loading every calendar, video, CRM, and payment package even when the caller only needs one (for example deletePayment or a single getCalendar). That keeps the cold-start and memory cost of the old static barrel and adds a burst of parallel module loads. Each import() promise is also stored with no .catch(). If any app module rejects and that key is not awaited, the rejection is unhandled; Node's default unhandledRejection behavior throws and can exit the process, including for an app the current request never uses. A failed optional app should not be able to crash the server. Lazy-load on first access and attach rejection handling so an unused or broken app degrades instead of rejecting in the background.

findings.title: Failed app import throws out of booking and availability flows
findings.body: getCalendar awaits appStore[calendarType] with no try/catch. A rejected dynamic import now throws, whereas a missing implementation previously returned null. CalendarManager.createEvent and updateEvent only catch errors from calendar.createEvent/updateEvent, not from getCalendar, so one broken app chunk fails the whole EventManager create/update instead of returning success: false for that credential. deleteEvent has the same gap. getCachedResults does Promise.all on every getCalendar call, so one rejected import fails busy-time lookup for every connected calendar. That can 500 availability, or, if an upstream caller treats the failure as no busy data, hide conflicts and allow double booking. Catch import failures in getCalendar and return null, which callers already handle as "calendar not implemented".

findings.title: getCalendar promises are started and sometimes discarded
findings.body: getCalendar is now async, but getCalendarCredentials still calls it synchronously inside flatMap, before the app.variant === "calendar" check. When the variant is not calendar (types ending in _calendar still enter this filter, including *_other_calendar apps), the returned promise is dropped. If that promise rejects — getCalendar awaits a dynamic import that can reject — nothing handles it, which is an unhandledRejection introduced by this change. When the promise is kept, the exported calendar field silently changed from a Calendar instance to Promise<Calendar | null> while getCalendarCredentials stayed synchronous. getConnectedCalendars was updated to await item.calendar, but any other caller that still invokes calendar.listCalendars() without awaiting will throw at runtime. Only call getCalendar when the result is retained, and attach a catch (or await it) on every promise that is started.
